overlap.title: “A virgin shall conceive, and bear a son” — which child does Isaiah 7:14 mean?
overlap.summary: Isaiah 7:14 gives Ahaz a sign: “a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel”. The verses quoted do not say who the woman is, when the child is born, or whether he is the child of 8:3–4.
overlap.reasoning: The sign is given to “you”, the house of David (7:13–14); verse 16 says that before “the child” knows to refuse the evil “the land that thou abhorrest shall be forsaken of both her kings”. The verses name no mother and no father, and give no year. In chapter 8 the prophet goes to “the prophetess”, who conceives and bears a son named Mahershalalhashbaz, and verse 4 gives a similar timing (“before the child shall have knowledge to cry, My father, and my mother”); verse 8 addresses “O Immanuel”, and verse 18 says the prophet and “the children whom the Lord hath given me” are signs. Possible readings: a child born in the time of Ahaz to a woman of the court or of the prophet’s household, whom the text does not name; the child of 8:3–4 under another name; or a child still future from Ahaz’s time. The record does not decide between them.
overlap.scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. The question is limited to the verses quoted; the word search covers the packaged KJV text of Isaiah 1–27 only and is a word search. The record does not say that any reading is the right one, does not rest on the Hebrew or the Greek, and does not examine how another book uses the verse.

studies.title: Can God be seen?
studies.summary: Exodus describes Moses speaking with God “face to face”; John says no one has seen God. The tension depends on whether “face to face” means literal sight.

studies.title: Judas and the field of blood
studies.summary: Matthew and Acts give different accounts of Judas's death and the field purchase.

studies.title: Water or ground: the animals’ origin
studies.summary: Genesis 1 can sound like birds came from water, while Genesis 2 says ground. The apparent conflict depends on how Genesis 1:20 is translated.

studies.title: Plants before people—or after?
studies.summary: Genesis 1 places vegetation before people; Genesis 2 describes no field plants before a cultivator. Whether this conflicts depends on which plants are meant.

studies.title: David’s census: two different totals
studies.summary: The census totals differ: Israel is 800,000 versus 1.1 million; Judah is 500,000 versus 470,000. Different counting rules are proposed but not established here.

studies.title: Herod, Quirinius, and the birth chronology
studies.summary: Matthew places Jesus’s birth under Herod; Luke links it to Quirinius’s census. The historical chronology creates a tension if the same census is intended.
